Cloud-OpsBench: A Reproducible Benchmark for Agentic Root Cause Analysis in Cloud Systems

Abstract.

The transition to agentic Root Cause Analysis (RCA) necessitates benchmarks that evaluate active reasoning rather than passive classification. However, current frameworks fail to reconcile ecological validity with reproducibility. We introduce Cloud-OpsBench, a large-scale benchmark that employs a State Snapshot Paradigm to construct a deterministic digital twin of the cloud, featuring 452 distinct fault cases across 40 root cause types spanning the full Kubernetes stack. Crucially, Cloud-OpsBench serves as an enabling infrastructure for next-generation SRE research: (1) As a Data Engine, it harvests high-quality reasoning trajectories to bootstrap Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) for Small Language Models; (2) As an Reinforcement Learning (RL) environment, it transforms high-risk operations into a safe low-latency sandbox for training policy optimization agents; and (3) As a Diagnostic Standard, its process-centric protocol uncovers architectural bottlenecks guiding the design of robust specialized multi-agent system for RCA.

Keywords: 
Large Language Models, Cloud Computing, Root Cause Analysis, Benchmark, Agentic AI

1. Introduction

The reliability of cloud-native systems constitutes the foundation of modern online services (Yu et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2021). However, system complexity makes Root Cause Analysis (RCA) notoriously difficult (Li et al., 2022a; Chen et al., 2020). Traditional discriminative Artificial Intelligence for IT Operations (AIOps) models (e.g., VAEs) detect anomalies but lack the semantic understanding to explain failures (Xie et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2022; Hu et al., 2022). Recently, Large Language Models (LLMs) have triggered a paradigm shift towards Agentic RCA (Chen et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024). Unlike passive classifiers, these agents function as autonomous SREs, actively interacting with systems to verify hypotheses. This transition necessitates benchmarks that evaluate active diagnostic reasoning rather than static pattern recognition.

However, existing frameworks fail to balance ecological validity and reproducibility. (1) Static Telemetry Benchmarks (e.g., LogHub (Zhu et al., 2023), RCAEval (Pham et al., 2025)) rely on retrospective data dumps. They reduce agents to passive readers, ignoring the essential capability of interactive tool use. (2) Dynamic Environment Benchmarks (e.g., AIOpsLab (Chen et al., 2025)) deploy live microservices but suffer from stochasticity. Non-deterministic factors (e.g., network jitter) introduce noise, rendering rigorous A/B testing impossible. Furthermore, reliance on outcome-based metrics (e.g., Accuracy@1) rewards spurious guesses, failing to distinguish systematic reasoning from statistical probability.

To bridge this gap, we present Cloud-OpsBench, the first large-scale reproducible benchmark on Kubernetes for Agentic RCA. At its core is the State Snapshot Paradigm, which functions as a deterministic digital twin. Instead of relying on transient live clusters (Sun et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025), Cloud-OpsBench freezes the complete operational context (control plane objects, metrics, logs) into an immutable persistence layer. Interaction is reconstructed via a mocked interface simulating standard tools (e.g., kubectl) with zero latency. This design guarantees 100% reproducibility while supporting complex tool usage. Cloud-OpsBench comprises 452 distinct fault cases across 40 fault types, covering the full Kubernetes stack.

Crucially, we position Cloud-OpsBench not merely as a leaderboard, but as an enabling infrastructure for next-generation SRE research. Our empirical evaluation serves to validate its utility in three key dimensions: (1) As a Data Engine, it demonstrates that procedural demonstrations outperform declarative knowledge, proving its value in harvesting trajectories to bootstrap Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT); (2) As a Diagnostic Standard, its process-centric protocol uncovers architectural bottlenecks (e.g., “Redundancy Paradox” in DeepSeek-V3.2 and “Syntactic Fragility” in Qwen-14B) guiding the design of specialized multi-agent swarms; (3) As an RL Environment, its deterministic nature provides the necessary stability for training future agents via policy optimization.

In summary, this paper makes the following contributions:

  • •

    A Process-Centric Evaluation Paradigm. We propose Cloud-OpsBench, the first white-box benchmark for Agentic RCA. By quantifying trajectory alignment, we demonstrate that how an agent verifies is as critical as what it concludes, establishing a new standard for reliability.

  • •

    An Enabling Data Engine for Model Bootstrapping. We establish Cloud-OpsBench as a high-quality data engine. By validating that 14B-parameter models using our procedural demonstrations can rival proprietary giants, we provide a cost-efficient blueprint for bootstrapping private SRE agents via SFT.

  • •

    A Safe Sandbox for Policy Optimization. We construct a high-fidelity Digital Twin that transforms AIOps from a risky operational task into a safe low-latency learning environment. This unlocks the capability to train agents via RL to dynamically optimize exploration strategies.

2. Motivation and Challenges

2.1. The Paradigm Shift: From Statistical Detection to Agentic Root Cause Analysis

The field of AIOps is currently undergoing a fundamental transition from discriminative artificial intelligence to generative agents. This shift represents a change in both the definition of failure and the mechanism of diagnosis. In the era dominated by deep learning, failures were primarily defined as statistical deviations (Yu et al., 2023; Li et al., 2022b; Yu et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2024). The objective of traditional AIOps models (e.g., VAEs (Xie et al., 2023), LSTMs (Li et al., 2023)) was to model the normal distribution of system metrics. In this context, RCA were treated as curve-fitting or classification tasks (Zhang et al., 2022; Hu et al., 2022), where the goal was to identify data points that diverged significantly from historical baselines. The emergence of LLMs has redefined the problem (Li et al., 2025; Ahmed et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024). The focus has moved toward identifying the logical conflicts between observed states and expected behaviors defined in system protocols (Yang et al., 2025; Mao et al., 2025).

Consequently, the role of the AI model has evolved from passive classifiers to autonomous SREs. Unlike their predecessors, these agentic SREs must possess three critical operational competencies:

  • •

    Active Perception: The ability to proactively query system states via tools rather than passively ingesting dumps.

  • •

    Knowledge Grounding: The capacity to synthesize telemetry with external documentation.

  • •

    Deductive Reasoning: The capability to verify hypotheses through multi-step logic.

However, existing benchmarks (Yu et al., 2023; AIOPS.CN, 2021; AIOPS.CN, 2020; Si et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024; Cui et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2025; Pham et al., 2025) largely remain aligned with the previous paradigm of statistical pattern recognition (details shown in Table 1). This discrepancy creates a significant threat to construct validity. As detailed in the following sections, current benchmarks fail to adequately measure the specific capabilities required for Agentic RCA across three critical dimensions: data modality, environmental interaction, and evaluation metrics.

2.2. Gap 1: The Ecological Validity Gap in Static Telemetry Artifacts

To function as an SRE, an agent must interact with the system. However, most existing benchmarks, such as TimeSeriesBench (Si et al., 2024), LogHub (Zhu et al., 2023), RCAEval (Pham et al., 2025), and LogEval (Cui et al., 2025), are fundamentally constructed upon static telemetry artifacts, as illustrated in Fig. 1(a). These artifacts are retrospective collections of logs, metrics, or traces that have been dumped and stored after an incident has occurred. These retrospective collections of logs or metrics effectively strip away the environment, reducing the agent from an engineer to a reader. This static paradigm fails to motivate or measure the core competencies of Agentic RCA in three ways:

1. Interaction Constraints. Real-world SREs rely on defined APIs (e.g., kubectl) to actively investigate issues. In contrast, benchmarks like LogHub or RCAEval provide only raw data files without execution interfaces. This absence forces the model to process entire datasets essentially as a reading comprehension task. This setup implicitly assumes the agent is a passive entity with infinite context, which contradicts the reality of large-scale operations where telemetry exceeds gigabytes per hour. By denying the agent the ability to retrieve information, existing benchmarks fail to evaluate the critical skill of information seeking efficiency.

2. Modality Mismatch. Human experts rarely parse raw high-dimensional tensors; they rely on monitoring tools to abstract signals into semantic events (e.g., “Latency spike detected”) (Yu et al., 2026). Existing benchmarks, however, force a bottom-up, perception-heavy approach, requiring agents to parse thousands of metric points. This conflates signal processing with diagnostic reasoning. A motivated agentic benchmark should assess whether an agent can interpret high-level system states, not whether it can perform arithmetic on CSV rows.

3. Knowledge Vacuum. Benchmarks based on toy systems (e.g., Train Ticket (Zhou et al., 2018)) typically provide only runtime data, creating a knowledge vacuum. This setup ignores the fact that human operators rely heavily on external knowledge sources, including troubleshooting guides, API documentation, and system topology diagrams. Without access to system specifications or known failure patterns, agents are forced to rely on parametric knowledge or speculation rather than grounded logical reasoning.

2.3. Gap 2: The Reproducibility Challenge in Dynamic Environments

Recognizing the limitations of static artifacts, recent research has pivoted toward dynamic evaluation frameworks (Chen et al., 2025; Jha et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2025) that deploy actual microservices and inject faults in real time. As shown in Fig. 1(b), while this approach improves fidelity, it introduces a critical trade-off regarding reproducibility and efficiency.

The primary obstacle is the inherent non-determinism of live cloud systems. In a cloud system, the manifestation of a fault is heavily influenced by non-deterministic factors. For instance, a network delay injection of 500 milliseconds may trigger a cascade of timeouts in one experimental run but result in a seamless retry in another. This environmental volatility undermines the fairness of comparative evaluations. In a scientific benchmark, the test conditions must be invariant across different models. If Model A fails due to a transient network jitter while Model B succeeds because the network was stable, the comparison is invalid. Current dynamic frameworks fail to decouple intrinsic system complexity from experimental noise, rendering rigorous A/B testing impossible.

Beyond stochasticity, the operational overhead of dynamic environments creates a prohibitive barrier to entry. Maintaining a high-fidelity cluster requires substantial cloud resources, but more critically, it imposes excessive verification latency. A single evaluation cycle comprising system deployment, fault injection, agent execution, and environment restoration is inherently slow. Running a comprehensive benchmark on live systems can consume dozens of machine hours per iteration (Zhang et al., 2025). This prolonged feedback loop drastically hinders the iterative development of agent strategies, making essential tasks like prompt refinement and hyperparameter tuning practically infeasible for researchers without industrial-scale infrastructure.

2.4. Gap 3: The Evaluation Gap in Outcome-Oriented Metrics

Even if data and environmental challenges are resolved, the prevailing metrics used in AIOps benchmarks remain a bottleneck. The majority of existing studies continue to rely on standard classification metrics, such as Precision, Recall, and F1-score (Sun et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2023; Pham et al., 2025). While these metrics are effective for discriminative models where the goal is a single label prediction, they exhibit a severe outcome bias when applied to generative agents. This bias obscures the critical distinction between genuine reasoning and spurious guessing.

The core limitation is that outcome-oriented metrics fail to scrutinize the intermediate reasoning process (Wang et al., 2026; Kartik et al., 2025). LLMs are known to be susceptible to hallucinations and can exploit shortcuts in the data distribution. It is possible for an agent to identify the correct root cause based on a completely erroneous logical path, a phenomenon often described as being right for the wrong reasons. For instance, an agent might correctly flag a database service as the culprit not because it retrieved and analyzed the relevant latency metrics, but simply because the database component appeared frequently in the historical training data associated with generic error keywords.

A benchmark that only evaluates the final output assigns a perfect score to such unreliable behavior. This validates a diagnostic process that lacks grounding in evidence. In a real-time diagnostic task, the value of an agent lies not just in its conclusion, but in the efficiency and logical coherence of its investigation. Current metrics are blind to the quality of the investigation. They treat a “logical but failed” diagnosis equivalent to a “hallucinated and failed” one. Consequently, a comprehensive evaluation must shift focus from calculating simple prediction accuracy to quantifying reasoning alignment and efficiency, ensuring that the agent follows a logical evidence-based trajectory similar to that of a human expert (Wang et al., 2026; Gulli et al., 2025).

2.5. Bridging the Gaps: Requirements for Benchmarking Agentic RCA

The transition to Agentic RCA has exposed a dilemma: researchers are currently forced to choose between static artifacts (reproducible but unrealistic) and live environments (realistic but unstable). To resolve this and align benchmarking with the true motivation of enabling the Agentic RCA, we identify three design requirements:

  1. •

    High-Fidelity Interaction with Deterministic Replay: The environment must support essential SRE tool-use capabilities (e.g., kubectl) to enable active information seeking, while simultaneously guaranteeing deterministic state transitions. This necessitates a shift from live execution to state snapshotting, where the system state is frozen and served via mock interfaces to ensure zero-cost and 100% reproducible evaluations.

  2. •

    Knowledge-Augmented Context: To bridge the epistemic void, the benchmark must integrate system and operational knowledge (e.g., system documents, troubleshooting guides) alongside telemetry. The objective is not merely to evaluate retrieval mechanics, but to assess the agent’s capacity for knowledge-grounded reasoning. Specifically, how well it synthesizes external information to diagnose novel issues in an open-book setting.

  3. •

    Process-Oriented Evaluation: Assessment protocols must move beyond binary success/failure labels. A rigorous benchmark should quantify the alignment of the diagnosis trajectory, penalizing agents that hallucinate evidence or execute illogical query sequences, even if they accidentally arrive at the correct root cause.

3. Cloud-OpsBench

To address the limitations of existing benchmarks, we present Cloud-OpsBench. As illustrated in Fig. 2, Cloud-OpsBench is designed as a high-fidelity, deterministic, and process-oriented benchmark. It comprises 452 distinct fault cases spanning 40 specific cloud fault types, covering the full Kubernetes stack. The core innovation of Cloud-OpsBench lies in its architectural alignment with the requirements identified in Section 2.5:

  1. •

    Addressing Gap 1: We utilize a high-fidelity Kubernetes testbed (§ 3.3.1) and a knowledge-rich fault generation pipeline (§ 3.3.2) to ensure agents operate in a realistic open-book context.

  2. •

    Addressing Gap 2: We introduce the State Snapshot paradigm (§ 3.2), which freezes the crime scene into a deterministic Digital Twin, eliminating noise while preserving interactivity.

  3. •

    Addressing Gap 3: We formalize the task as a trajectory-based decision process (§ 3.1) and synthesize canonical reference trajectories, enabling the assessment of reasoning logic rather than just final outcomes.

3.1. Agentic RCA Task Formulation

To rigorously evaluate both the outcome accuracy and the process validity of SRE agents, we formalize the Agentic RCA task as a trajectory-based decision process. We define the ground truth as a tuple ℛ∗=⟨S,C,R⟩\mathcal{R}^{*}=\langle S,C,R\rangle (denoting Stage, Component, and Root Cause) and a set of expert reference trajectories {𝒯∗}\{\mathcal{T}^{*}\}. Formally, the agentic diagnosis is modeled as a mapping function ff that produces a composite output:

(1) f:⟨Aa​l​e​r​t,ℰs​n​a​p​s​h​o​t⟩→⟨𝒯,ℛ^⟩.f:\langle A_{alert},\mathcal{E}_{snapshot}\rangle\rightarrow\langle\mathcal{T},\hat{\mathcal{R}}\rangle.

This process consists of three distinct phases:

1. Input Space: The agent receives a natural language alert Aa​l​e​r​tA_{alert} (e.g., “Service unreachable”)and access to a cached system snapshot ℰs​n​a​p​s​h​o​t\mathcal{E}_{snapshot}. Crucially, ℰs​n​a​p​s​h​o​t\mathcal{E}_{snapshot} serves as a deterministic high-fidelity cache of the system state, enabling the agent to execute interactive queries (e.g., kubectl logs) without stochastic noise.

2. Diagnostic Trajectory (𝒯\mathcal{T}): The agent interacts with the environment to generate a reasoning trajectory 𝒯=[(t1,a1,o1),…,(tn,an,on)]\mathcal{T}=[(t_{1},a_{1},o_{1}),\dots,(t_{n},a_{n},o_{n})]. At each step ii:

  • •

    Thought (tit_{i}): The agent analyzes the current context to formulate a hypothesis.

  • •

    Action (aia_{i}): The agent issues a tool call to probe ℰs​n​a​p​s​h​o​t\mathcal{E}_{snapshot}.

  • •

    Observation (oio_{i}): The environment returns the pre-recorded execution result.

This trajectory 𝒯\mathcal{T} is treated as part of the system output to enable process-oriented evaluation.

3. Output Space: Upon concluding the investigation, the agent yields a final result consisting of:

  • •

    Trajectory (𝒯\mathcal{T}): The complete sequence of investigative actions, which is evaluated against expert trajectories {𝒯∗}\{\mathcal{T}^{*}\} for procedural alignment.

  • •

    Predicted Diagnosis (ℛ^\hat{\mathcal{R}}): The final structured tuple identifying the root cause, which is evaluated against the ground truth ℛ∗\mathcal{R}^{*} for outcome accuracy.

3.2. Design Philosophy: The State Snapshot Paradigm

The core design philosophy of Cloud-OpsBench addresses the fundamental tension between reproducibility and ecological validity (§ 2). To bridge this gap, we introduce the State Snapshot paradigm (depicted in Fig. 1(c)), which conceptually serves as a deterministic digital twin of the target system at the precise moment of failure. Unlike traditional static artifacts (Gap 1)(§ 2), a State Snapshot captures the holistic operational context. This encompasses not only historical telemetry (e.g., logs, metrics) but also the static control plane configurations (e.g., Kubernetes manifests) and the instantaneous data plane states (e.g., Kubernetes pod lists), thereby freezing the complete environmental context required for diagnosis.

The fundamental innovation of this paradigm lies in the decoupling of state storage from tool interaction. In dynamic benchmarks, system state is transient and tightly coupled to a runtime environment. In contrast, our approach freezes this state into immutable persistence layers, eliminating environmental noise. Interactivity is then reconstructed via a mocked operational interface that acts as a deterministic translation layer. When an agent executes a command like kubectl get pods, it does not query a volatile API server but rather retrieves data from the frozen snapshot.

This architecture enables standard tool-use within a strictly deterministic environment. By simulating the behavior of native CLI tools on top of static data, Cloud-OpsBench ensures high-fidelity interaction where agents operate exactly as human SREs would, while guaranteeing reproducibility. Every execution yields the exact same output regardless of external factors, allowing for rigorous repetitive evaluation of agentic reasoning trajectories.

3.3. Benchmark Construction

As illustrated in Figure 2, we design a pipeline that bridges unstructured operational knowledge with deterministic runtime environments. This pipeline integrates a human-verified knowledge base with a Multi-Agent System (MAS) to generate the final dataset of 452 distinct fault cases.

3.3.1. Benchmark Testbed

Before detailing the generation pipeline, we first introduce the target cloud-native environment. To ensure ecological validity, we establish a high-fidelity testbed on Huawei Cloud ECS. The testbed operates on a Kubernetes cluster (v1.31) hosted on 4 instances. As the foundation of cloud-native infrastructure, Kubernetes offers not only a complex distributed control plane for fault injection but also a standardized corpus of documentation. This allows us to rigorously test knowledge-grounded reasoning, distinguishing our approach from benchmarks based on proprietary or obscure systems. Integrated within this infrastructure is a lightweight native observability plane designed to support the State Snapshot mechanism. Specifically, we deploy Prometheus (Prometheus, 2026) and Istio (Istio, 2026) to capture metrics (e.g., CPU Usage) which power the anomaly detection tools. Furthermore, we leverage the native Kubernetes API to directly expose real-time object states and retrieve on-demand container logs, ensuring low-latency access for resource inspection and log analysis.

To stimulate this infrastructure, we deploy Google Online Boutique (Google, 2026), the de facto standard benchmark for cloud-native research. We select this workload not for its specific business logic, but for its structural representativeness as a cloud-native systems proxy. It comprises 11 polyglot microservices communicating via gRPC, covering a wide spectrum of generic operational patterns (e.g., synchronous RPC, asynchronous queuing, and caching). By employing a load generator (Locust(Locust, 2026)) to simulate continuous user traffic, we utilize the application purely as a “canary in the coal mine”: its latency and error rates serve as high-level indicators of the underlying platform instability (e.g., node exhaustion or network partition) that our agents aim to diagnose. Complementing this setup, we integrate ChaosBlade (Chaosblade, 2026) for infrastructure-level perturbations (e.g., network loss, disk pressure) and utilize atomic kubectl commands for configuration mutations, ensuring the benchmark covers the full spectrum of cloud reliability challenges.

3.3.2. Phase 1: Fault Knowledge Base Construction

To comprehensively evaluate the diagnostic capabilities of Agentic RCA, we collect a diverse fault dataset by synthesizing information from multiple complementary sources. First, we extracted specification-based misconfigurations from official Kubernetes documentation and deployment tutorials(k8sdoc, 2025), which clarify deterministic relationships between configuration parameters and potential failure consequences (e.g., incorrect service selector resulting in traffic routing failures). Second, we extracted empirical operational faults from developer communities (e.g., Stack Overflow)(stackoverflow, 2025; KodeKloud, 2025), capturing errors frequently encountered by users. Finally, we supplemented these with established academic paper (Barletta et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025; Jha et al., 2025) to ensure coverage of widely recognized canonical failure modes in the AIOps community.

Raw data from these sources are typically unstructured and combine narrative prose with fragmented code snippets. To transform this into a usable knowledge base, we leverage Gemini 3 Pro, a state-of-the-art LLM, to extract structured metadata via few-shot prompting. We define a uniform fault reproduction model composed of two core dimensions:

  • •

    Semantic Metadata: This component includes the fault name, a symptom description, and the root cause logic. These details provide the agent with natural language context to understand the causality chain (e.g., Pod remains Pending because node taints block scheduling).

  • •

    Deployment Artifacts: To ensure deterministic execution, we formalize the reproduction steps into a tuple ⟨𝒫,𝒜,𝒮⟩\langle\mathcal{P},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{S}\rangle.(i) Prerequisites (𝒫\mathcal{P}) capture the necessary cluster state pre-injection (e.g., ResourceQuotas); (ii) Fault Artifact (𝒜\mathcal{A}) represents the core defective configuration (e.g., a misconfigured YAML) or the active injection rule (e.g., a ChaosBlade command); (iii) Activation Sequence (𝒮\mathcal{S}) defines the ordered operations to apply 𝒫\mathcal{P} and 𝒜\mathcal{A}.

To ensure the accuracy and practical utility of the Fault Knowledge Base, we validate both the semantic quality of fault descriptions and reproducibility of faults. First, we employ an LLM-as-a-Judge(Zheng et al., 2023) mechanism base on Gemini 3 Pro to iteratively score and refine the fault descriptions, thereby enhancing their technical accuracy and readability for humans. These pre-filtered candidates are then presented to cloud-native experts for the final review. As illustrated in Figure 2, experts focus on validating the semantic logic of root causes and refining the technical details of the deployment artifacts. Finally, to verify execution fidelity, we deploy the approved artifacts in a sandbox cluster, confirming that the formalized model ⟨𝒫,𝒜,𝒮⟩\langle\mathcal{P},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{S}\rangle consistently triggers expected symptoms. Only entries passing this triad of checks (LLM Judge →\to Human Expert →\to Runtime Verification) are committed to the final Knowledge Base. Finally, we build a comprehensive fault knowledge base organized around the rigorous taxonomy detailed in Table 2. Our taxonomy encompasses 7 distinct fault categories spanning the full Kubernetes stack. Within these categories, we define 40 specific root cause types, ensuring fine-grained coverage.

3.3.3. Phase 2: Automatic Fault Case Generation

Traditional fault injection relies heavily on manual orchestration, which is labor-intensive and unscalable. To automate this, we employ a Multi-Agent System (MAS) that mirrors a collaborative engineering team. As illustrated in Fig. 2, the system orchestrates three agents in a closed loop to transform static fault knowledge into reproducible benchmark cases.

1. Generation-Correction Loop.

The core workflow operates as a closed-loop iterative process designed to overcome the inherent resilience of cloud systems. The cycle initiates with Generator Agent, acting as the architect. By synthesizing the structured fault knowledge with real-time cluster info, it employs Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning to construct a precise fault reproduction triplet ℳ=⟨𝒫,𝒜,𝒮⟩\mathcal{M}=\langle\mathcal{P},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{S}\rangle, which encapsulates the prerequisites, fault artifact, and activation sequence.

This model is immediately operationalized by Executor Agent, which serves as the infrastructure interface. It translates the abstract activation sequence 𝒮\mathcal{S} into imperative low-level operations (e.g., applying Kubernetes manifests via kubectl or executing chaos scripts) and strictly enforces the deployment order to ensure the fault is physically injected into the live Kubernetes environment.

Following execution, Verifier Agent continuously monitors telemetry to perform a rigorous validation check. Crucially, if the injection fails to trigger the expected anomaly, which is often due to Kubernetes automatically masking the fault (e.g., rescheduling a Pod to bypass a taint), Verifier Agent diagnoses the discrepancy between the intended logic and the actual runtime state. It then instructs Generator Agent to refine the injection parameters (e.g., increasing resource stress intensity). This self-correcting loop persists until the fault is reliably verified, ensuring that every generated case is ecologically valid.

2. State Snapshot.

Upon verification, the State Snapshot module materializes the paradigm proposed in Section 3.2. The system freezes the crime scene by preserving raw telemetry (a fixed window of metrics, logs, and objects). To construct the mocked operational interface, we perform an exhaustive parameter sweep using our diagnostic toolset (T1–T10, Table 3). The module pre-executes every plausible diagnostic command against the frozen data, effectively pre-rendering the Digital Twin’s responses:

  • •

    Resource Enumeration: The system iterates through all standard Kubernetes objects (e.g., Pods, Services, PVCs) in the target namespace. For every identified object, it executes retrieval tools (T1, T2) to capture their full specifications, runtime statuses, and events.

  • •

    Service Topology & Telemetry: For each registered service, the system executes diagnostic tools to freeze its application state. This includes: (i) running reachability checks (T6) against target service ports; (ii) fetching static configurations (T3) and dependency graphs (T4); and (iii) extracting and analyzing logs via both raw retrieval (T5) and error pattern summary (T9).

  • •

    Cluster-Wide Context: To capture the global context, the system scans all nodes to record hardware capacity, metadata (T7) and cluster component health (T10), while processing all raw metrics into structured anomaly alerts (T8).

The resulting JSON repository serves as the immutable persistence layer. To ensure the snapshot effectively covers the investigative search space, we enforce a Maximum Information Coverage strategy. On average, each fault case generates 487 distinct tool invocations. This exhaustive pre-computation guarantees that valid agent queries (e.g., correct service names and ports) will hit a deterministic entry, while invalid queries (e.g., non-existent pods) map to realistic Not Found errors, thereby faithfully simulating the boundaries of a live system.

Crucially, this finite set of pre-computed states does not trivialize the diagnostic challenge. We design the interaction paradigm to enforce combinatorial complexity rather than atomic selection. First, the agent operates in an open-ended generation setting. Since the mock interface simulates an infinite parameter space by returning realistic errors for invalid inputs, the agent must syntactically generate precise commands rather than selecting from a closed menu. Second, a successful diagnosis requires a coherent chain of interdependent steps (typically N≈10N\approx 10), creating a reasoning search space of 487N487^{N}. This combinatorial explosion ensures that random guessing is statistically impossible, thereby maintaining the benchmark’s rigor as a test of systematic deductive logic.

3. Ground Truth Annotation.

To evaluate both the final diagnosis and the investigative process, the module automatically synthesizes a ground truth tuple 𝒢∗=⟨ℛ∗,𝒯∗⟩\mathcal{G}^{*}=\langle\mathcal{R}^{*},\mathcal{T}^{*}\rangle. The first component, the true root cause (ℛ∗\mathcal{R}^{*}), is derived directly from the Generator Agent’s design intent, specifying the exact location (e.g., node-1) and fault category to serve as the gold standard for evaluating diagnosis accuracy.

To support process-oriented evaluation, we synthesize a canonical diagnostic path by inverting the injection logic. Since Generator Agent possesses omniscient knowledge of the fault artifact 𝒜\mathcal{A}, we employ a rule-based engine to deterministically map the injected fault (e.g., “Added a Taint”) to the specific verification step required to reveal it (e.g., “Execute describe node tool”). This inversion process yields a critical evidence chain that serves as the logical skeleton for the ground truth, structured around two design principles: (i) Strict Causal Precedence (Anti-Guessing): We define the trajectory not merely as a set of actions, but as a directed graph where symptom discovery (identifying the observable anomaly) is a logical prerequisite for root cause verification (confirming the defect). This structure ensures that the ground truth captures the full deductive chain, distinguishing valid reasoning from unfounded shortcuts. (ii) Exploratory Noise Tolerance (Pro-Redundancy): Recognizing that realistic troubleshooting involves trial-and-error, we define 𝒯∗\mathcal{T}^{*} as a minimal mandatory subsequence rather than a rigid script. This definition inherently accommodates interstitial heuristic actions (e.g., checking logs that turn out to be empty), ensuring that the ground truth represents the necessity of evidence without excluding the reality of exploration.

4. Evaluation

In this section, we evaluate LLM agents on Cloud-OpsBench to answer the following RQs:

  1. •

    RQ1 (Outcome Effectiveness): How accurately can LLM agents diagnose root causes?

  2. •

    RQ2 (Process Alignment): Do agents follow human expert diagnostic paths?

  3. •

    RQ3 (Tool Robustness): How robust are LLM agents in invoking diagnostic tools?

  4. •

    RQ4 (Knowledge Efficacy): Does external knowledge improve diagnostic performance?

4.1. Experimental Setup

The evaluating agent framework is implemented in Python 3.10, utilizing CrewAI(CrewAI, 2025) as the orchestration engine and Pydantic(Pydantic, 2026) for structured tool interface definitions. Consistent with white-box design principles, we employ Langfuse(Langfuse, 2025) for comprehensive agent observability, which automatically captures detailed traces of LLM generations, reasoning steps, and tool invocations during the diagnostic process.

We evaluate the benchmark using seven models, explicitly categorized into two tiers to assess the impact of parameter scale. The Large Language Models tier comprises high-capacity frontier models, including proprietary leaders (GPT-5, GPT-4o, Claude-4-Sonnet) and open-source giants (DeepSeek-V3.2, Qwen3-235B). In contrast, the Small Language Models (SLMs) tier (Zhong et al., 2025) represents efficiency-optimized baselines with parameters under 20B, specifically Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-8B.

4.2. Evaluation Metrics

To provide a holistic assessment, we evaluate performance across two dimensions: Outcome Effectiveness and Process Quality. Unlike prior works (Jha et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025; Pham et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2023) that only rely on outcome-based metrics which inadvertently reward lucky guesses, our framework quantifies the logical fidelity of the diagnosis. By aligning the agent’s trajectory with expert-annotated paths (§ 3.3.3), we distinguish systematic reasoning from stochastic trial-and-error.

4.2.1. Outcome-based Metrics

These metrics evaluate the final diagnostic conclusion. A diagnosis is considered correct only if it strictly matches the ground truth ℛ∗\mathcal{R}^{*} in three dimensions: fault lifecycle stage, faulty component, and failure reason.

  1. •

    Top-k Accuracy Rate (A​@​kA@k)(Yu et al., 2021; Pham et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2023): This measures the probability that the correct root cause is included in agent’s top-kk predictions. Let r​circ_{i} denote the set of ground truth for the ii-th case, and EikE^{k}_{i} be the top-kk predicted elements. The metric is defined as: A​@​k=1|I|​∑i=1|I|𝕀⁡(r​ci⊆Eik)A@k=\frac{1}{|I|}\sum_{i=1}^{|I|}\mathbb{I}(rc_{i}\subseteq E^{k}_{i}). We evaluate with k=1,3k=1,3. A higher A​@​kA@k indicates better accuracy in identifying root causes.

  2. •

    Task Completion Rate (TCR): Proxies the agent’s operational stability and instruction-following capability. It is defined as the ratio of episodes where the agent successfully outputs a structured diagnosis without crashing or violating the output schema.

4.2.2. Process-based Metrics

To quantify reasoning quality, we compare the agent’s tool execution trajectory Ta​g​e​n​t=[a1,…,an]T_{agent}=[a_{1},\dots,a_{n}] against the expert ground truth path Tg​o​l​d=[g1,…,gm]T_{gold}=[g_{1},\dots,g_{m}]. An action aia_{i} matches gjg_{j} if and only if both the tool name and critical arguments are identical. Let 𝒮T\mathcal{S}_{T} be the set of distinct tool calls in TT.

  • •

    Trajectory Alignment. We employ three strictness levels to evaluate how closely the agent mimics expert procedures (Gulli et al., 2025; Kartik et al., 2025): (1) Exact Match measures how exactly the agent replicate the expert’s sequence of tool invocations, with no deviations in action or order. This stringent metric reflects a scenario where only the canonical diagnostic path is considered correct. (2) Any-Order Match: measures functional completeness by checking whether all necessary diagnostic actions in the gold trajectory are present in the agent’s execution, regardless of order or extra steps. (3) In-Order Match measures whether the agent performs all essential diagnostic steps in the correct relative order, while allowing arbitrary extra actions.

  • •

    Tool Usage Efficiency. To assess the quality of tool selection independent of execution order, we measure Tool Relevance and Tool Coverage (Wang et al., 2026). Relevance (R​e​l​e​v​a​n​c​e=|𝒮a​g​e​n​t∩𝒮g​o​l​d||𝒮a​g​e​n​t|Relevance=\frac{|\mathcal{S}_{agent}\cap\mathcal{S}_{gold}|}{|\mathcal{S}_{agent}|}) quantifies the fraction of the agent’s tool invocations that align with expert practice, while Coverage (C​o​v​e​r​a​g​e=|𝒮a​g​e​n​t∩𝒮g​o​l​d||𝒮g​o​l​d|Coverage=\frac{|\mathcal{S}_{agent}\cap\mathcal{S}_{gold}|}{|\mathcal{S}_{gold}|}) measures the proportion of essential diagnostic tools that the agent successfully employed. To assess operational overhead, we measure diagnostic efficiency via Mean Time to Identify (MTTI) and Steps (total tool invocations). Lower values indicate faster and more concise troubleshooting.

  • •

    Operational Robustness. We define three penalty metrics to quantify distinct failure modes: (1) Invalid Action Count (IAC) counts the number of tool invocations in a diagnostic episode that fail due to malformed arguments, hallucinated parameters, or violations of the expected tool schema. (2) Redundant Action Rate (RAR) is the fraction of redundant actions without new context or state change, indicating either reasoning stagnation or excessive re-confirmation. (3) Zero-Tool Diagnosis Rate (ZTDR) quantifies speculative hallucination by measuring the fraction of episodes where the agent directly generates a final result without performing any valid tool invocations, indicating reliance on parametric knowledge over evidence gathering.

4.3. RQ1: RCA Outcome Effectiveness

We present the evaluation results in Tab. 4 and Fig. 3. Tab. 4 provides a comparative analysis of seven LLM agents across outcome effectiveness and process quality metrics. Complementing this, Fig. 3 visualizes the performance distribution across seven specific fault scenarios.

High accuracy necessitates extensive exploration rather than rushed convergence. Our results indicate a positive correlation between diagnostic accuracy and the depth of exploration, challenging the assumption that shorter diagnosis implies higher efficiency. DeepSeek-V3.2 achieves the highest A​@​1A@1 (0.73) alongside the highest average step count (10.0) and Coverage (0.88). This pattern reflects an exhaustive verification strategy where the model systematically validates metrics, logs, and events. Conversely, GPT-4o demonstrates premature convergence. It records the lowest MTTI (23.27s) and shorter trajectories (5.67 steps) but yields significantly lower accuracy (A​@​1=0.49A@1=0.49). This divergence suggests that current agents lack an optimized termination mechanism calibrated for accuracy. Models employing redundant verification successfully identify complex root causes, whereas models prioritizing rapid conclusion often overlook critical evidence located deep within the system state.

Syntactic validity constitutes a primary bottleneck for SLMs. While reasoning capability is often considered the primary differentiator, our analysis reveals that SLM performance is constrained by fundamental tool-use correctness. Although the Task Completion Rate (TCR) remains high across all models (>0.82), the Invalid Action Count (IAC) metric exposes a significant disparity. SLMs such as Qwen3-14B exhibit an IAC of 0.40, which is approximately 10×10\times higher than that of GPT-5 (0.04). Trace analysis confirms that these models frequently generate invalid Kubernetes API payloads, such as referencing non-existent Pod names or producing malformed JSON. Unlike code generation tasks where compiler feedback is precise, runtime API errors are often ambiguous. Consequently, syntactic robustness functions as a strict prerequisite. An agent must possess the capability to generate valid queries to retrieve the telemetry required for subsequent reasoning.

Performance stratification is determined by symptom explicitness and observability. Diagnostic effectiveness varies significantly based on the logical distance between the symptom and the root cause. As visualized in the radar charts of Fig. 3, model performance follows a consistent trend across fault categories:

  • •

    Explicit Faults: In Startup and Runtime scenarios, agents achieve high accuracy (Avg A​@​1>0.65A@1>0.65). These faults produce explicit signals in Kubernetes Events (e.g., CrashLoopBackOff or OOMKilled). The diagnosis primarily involves symptom matching, which requires mapping a visible error code to a known cause.

  • •

    Implicit Faults: Performance declines in Admission and Performance scenarios (Avg A​@​1<0.36A@1<0.36). In these cases, the root cause location (e.g., resource contention) is decoupled from the symptom manifestation. Resolution requires cross-layer causal inference to correlate application latency with underlying infrastructure metrics.

This stratification indicates that current agents are proficient at processing explicit telemetry logs but face challenges in establishing holistic system topology representations when errors are distributed or lack direct error signals.

4.4. RQ2: RCA Process Alignment

To determine whether agents mimic human experts or develop independent reasoning patterns, we analyze the alignment metrics in Table 4. The data reveals a significant divergence between RCA result and procedural mimicry.

Functional completeness consistently supersedes procedural linearity. Across all models, Any-Order Match scores consistently outperform In-Order Match scores (e.g., for Qwen3-235B, 0.41 vs. 0.38). This gap quantifies the exploration overhead. Agents typically perform the necessary verification steps required by the ground truth but often intersperse them with irrelevant or redundant actions. The substantial drop from Any-Order to In-Order alignment highlights that while agents are proficient at identifying what information is needed (Information Retrieval), they struggle to organize these actions into the logical, linear deductive chain (Logical Planning) characteristic of human experts.

Operational redundancy serves as a necessary mechanism for reliability. Conventional wisdom in software engineering prioritizes execution efficiency (minimizing steps). However, our data suggests a redundancy paradox in agentic reasoning. Comparing the Redundant Action Rate (RAR), the highest-performing model, DeepSeek-V3.2, exhibits a notable RAR of 0.11, indicating that 11% of its actions are redundant. As illustrated in Case #1 of Fig. 4, where DeepSeek diagnoses an Admission failure, the agent intersperses redundant verification steps (yellow nodes) with progressive diagnostic actions to confirm system states before isolating the root cause. In contrast, the underperforming GPT-4o shows a near-zero RAR of 0.02. This correlation implies that what appears as inefficiency is functionally cognitive self-correction. High-performing agents utilize redundant checks to confirm transient system states or validate hypotheses before committing to a conclusion. Conversely, agents that strictly optimize for non-redundant paths often suffer from fragile reasoning, lacking the verification loops necessary to filter out hallucinations.

Top-tier models exhibit divergent reasoning strategies. While both DeepSeek-V3.2 and GPT-5 achieve SOTA accuracy, their underlying process metrics reveal fundamentally different reasoning paradigms: (i) Coverage-Centric Strategy (DeepSeek-V3.2): This model adopts a brute-force approach, maximizing evidence collection. It records the highest Steps (10.0) and Coverage (0.88), ensuring that nearly all expert-defined critical information is retrieved. This strategy prioritizes recall over precision, accepting higher redundancy (RAR=0.11) to guarantee diagnostic safety. (2) Relevance-Centric Strategy (GPT-5): Conversely, GPT-5 mimics the efficiency of a seasoned expert. It achieves the highest Relevance (0.65) with significantly fewer steps (5.57). This indicates a high signal-to-noise ratio in tool selection, where the model filters out exploratory noise and targets critical system states directly. This divergence implies that there is a trade-off between the safety of exhaustive search and the efficiency of heuristic leaps.

Tool selection precision dissociates from diagnostic success in SLMs. Our analysis uncovers a competence illusion in SLMs. As shown in Table 4, Qwen3-14B achieves a Tool Relevance score of 0.63, matching that of the much larger GPT-4o (0.63) and nearly approaching GPT-5 (0.65). This indicates that the model possesses strong semantic knowledge regarding which tools are appropriate for a given context (Classifier Competence). However, this high relevance does not translate to outcome effectiveness (A​@​1=0.34A@1=0.34 vs. GPT-5’s 0.670.67). This gap suggests that the bottleneck for SLMs is not tool selection (identifying the right API) but information integration (interpreting the API response). While they can correctly identify the need to check logs, they fail to synthesize the returned log data into a causal chain, highlighting that tool selection and diagnostic reasoning are distinct capability layers that scale differently with model size.

4.5. RQ3: Tool Robustness

Robustness evaluates the agent’s ability to generate valid tool invocations and recover from runtime execution errors. We analyze the Invalid Action Count (IAC) and Zero-Tool Diagnosis Rate (ZTDR) alongside the qualitative behaviors visualized in Fig. 4.

Lack of self-correction capabilities leads to reasoning stagnation in SLMs. The critical differentiator between model tiers is not merely the occurrence of errors, but the ability to utilize runtime feedback for recovery. As illustrated in Case#2 of Fig. 4, when small models (e.g., Qwen3-14B) encounter an API error (e.g., Pod not found), they fail to interpret the error message as corrective feedback. Instead of revising the query, they enter a repetition loop, retrying the exact same invalid payload until the step limit is exhausted. In contrast, large-scale models like DeepSeek-V3.2 demonstrate reflective debugging, where they analyze the error trace and successfully reformulate the tool invocation in the subsequent step. This indicates that robustness is defined by the meta-cognitive loop of error handling, which is largely absent in sub-20B models.

Proprietary models exhibit laziness via speculative shortcuts. Robustness also encompasses the discipline to strictly adhere to evidence-based workflows. We identify a premature conclusion failure mode in Claude-4-Sonnet, quantifiable by its high ZTDR of 0.32. As depicted in Case#4 of Fig. 4, this model occasionally bypasses the investigation phase entirely, hallucinating a specific root cause (e.g., claiming “High Latency due to CPU”) based solely on the generic alert description. While this behavior reduces steps (Avg 4.25), it compromises reliability (A​@​1=0.5A@1=0.5). True robustness requires the agent to suppress the parametric urge to generate a probable answer and instead verify the system state through execution, ensuring that every diagnosis is backed by runtime telemetry.

Schema Hallucination undermines tool utility. Beyond syntax errors, we observe a semantic failure mode in mid-tier models termed schema hallucination (Case #3 in Fig. 4). Agents frequently invent non-existent parameters for valid tools (e.g., passing filters to parameter-less APIs). Unlike simple syntax errors, these hallucinations suggest a fundamental misalignment between the agent’s internal representation of the tool and the actual API definition. This decoupling prevents the agent from utilizing the toolset effectively, even when the reasoning intent is correct.

4.6. RQ4: Knowledge Efficacy

In this section, we evaluate three mainstream knowledge enhancement strategies against the zero-shot baseline: (i) Chain-of-Thought (CoT), which enforces a structured reasoning template (e.g., Status → Events →\to Config →\to Cluster) to guide pre-action planning. (ii) In-Context Learning (ICL), which retrieves 3 historical diagnostic traces from the same fault category, including tool invocations and outcomes as dynamic demonstrations. (iii) Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), which injects relevant knowledge from authoritative Kubernetes operations documentation (LearnKube.CN, 2025) to ground domain understanding. The results in Table 5 indicate that providing procedural demonstrations is more effective than providing declarative knowledge or encouraging abstract reasoning.

Procedural demonstration (ICL) outweighs declarative knowledge retrieval (RAG). A consistent trend across all models is the dominance of In-Context Learning (ICL). For GPT-4o, ICL improves A@1 from 0.49 to 0.7, significantly outperforming RAG (0.61). This performance gap illuminates the nature of the agentic bottleneck. RAG injects authoritative Kubernetes operations documentation, which helps agents understand what a tool does (enhancing Coverage), but fails to instruct how to orchestrate these tools in a multi-step diagnosis. In contrast, ICL retrieves historical diagnostic traces, providing concrete examples of valid tool invocations and outcome interpretations. This suggests that agents benefit more from mimicking the execution patterns of experts (Procedural Norms) than from reading the manuals of the system (Declarative Knowledge).

Few-shot demonstrations effectively bridge the scale gap for SLMs. One of the most profound findings is the disproportionate benefit ICL confers on SLMs. Under the Base setting, Qwen3-14B (A@1=0.34) lags far behind GPT-4o (0.49). However, with ICL, Qwen3-14B achieves a A@1 of 0.71, effectively matching or even surpassing the performance of the unprompted GPT-5 tier. Table 5 reveals the mechanism behind this resurrection: ICL significantly reduces the Invalid Action Count (IAC) for Qwen3-14B from 0.40 to 0.29. This indicates that SLMs possess latent reasoning capabilities that are suppressed by syntactic fragility. By observing valid tool invocation examples in the context window, SLMs can copy-paste the correct schema structure, bypassing the syntax barrier identified in RQ3 and unlocking their reasoning potential.

Structured reasoning templates (CoT) yield diminishing returns. Contrary to its success in logical reasoning tasks, the CoT strategy, which enforces a “Status →\to Events →\to Config” template, proves ineffective for Agentic RCA. For Qwen3-235B, CoT degrades performance (0.50 →\to 0.47), and for GPT-4o, it offers no gain. We attribute this to template rigidity and hallucination amplification. First, a fixed pre-action planning template may not align with the dynamic nature of diverse faults (e.g., a network issue requires a different flow than a crash loop). Second, without external grounding (like RAG or ICL), forcing a model to generate a long reasoning chain often induces it to hallucinate plausible but incorrect intermediate states. This indicates that reasoning structure alone is insufficient without the grounding of valid execution history or external knowledge.

5. Discussion

5.1. Significance and Impact

Redefining the Evaluation Standard for Autonomous SRE. Prior to Cloud-OpsBench, the field relied on outcome-based metrics that inadvertently rewarded stochastic guessing (Pham et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2023; AIOPS.CN, 2020; AIOPS.CN, 2021) . This work invalidates that approach. By enforcing a process-centric evaluation paradigm, we demonstrate that how an agent verifies is as critical as what it concludes. We establish the first rigorous standard for differentiating between fragile probability generation and robust systematic reasoning in industrial reliability tasks.

Diagnosing the Diagnosers. Beyond aggregate performance rankings, this work provides a rigorous taxonomy of failure mechanisms in Agentic RCA. We empirically isolate distinct cognitive deficits: Syntactic Fragility in SLMs and Parametric Hallucination in frontier models. This white-box analysis suggests that future improvements should focus on targeted interventions (e.g., syntax-constrained decoding or verification loops) rather than relying solely on parameter scaling.

Democratizing Research via Zero-Cost Replay. Prior to Cloud-OpsBench, the high barrier of entry which requires expensive cloud clusters and incurring lengthy feedback loops (often hours per run (Chen et al., 2025)) effectively gated Agentic RCA research to industrial labs with abundant resources. By decoupling system state from runtime execution, we reduce the evaluation cost from substantial cloud bills to negligible computation. Cloud-OpsBench enables a full-scale benchmark run in seconds on a standard laptop. This infrastructure empowers the broader academic community to iterate rapidly on agent designs without the friction of deployment overhead.

5.2. Future Research Opportunities

Cloud-OpsBench serves as an extensible environment for next-generation SRE research. We map our empirical insights to specific future research opportunities.

From Monolithic to Multi-Agent Architectures. Our identification of a competence mismatch where SLMs fail due to rigid schema compliance despite having sufficient semantic intuition proves that generic reasoning capability is not the sole bottleneck. To address this, future research can abandon the one-model-fits-all approach in favor of multi-agent architectures based on Cloud-OpsBench. For example, researchers can explore multi-agent architectures where roles are specialized: a planner agent (powered by robust models like GPT-5) orchestrates the diagnostic logic, while lightweight executor agents (fine-tuned SLMs) handle specific tool interactions, thereby optimizing the cost-accuracy trade-off.

From Open-Ended Prompting to RL Policies. The reasoning stagnation and premature convergence observed in RQ2 (§ 4.4) indicate that current agents operate as open-loop systems lacking an optimal stopping mechanism. By functioning as a high-fidelity Digital Twin, Cloud-OpsBench transforms AIOps into a safe reinforcement learning environment. We encourage researchers to utilize process metrics (Steps, RAR) as reward signals to train agents via PPO (Schulman et al., 2017) or DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023). This shifts the paradigm from static prompt engineering to dynamic policy optimization, allowing agents to learn exploration strategies that balance thoroughness with efficiency.

From Static Manuals to Self-Evolving Data Engines. Our RQ4 findings (§ 4.6) demonstrate that procedural demonstrations (ICL) significantly outperform declarative documentation (RAG), suggesting that SRE knowledge is best represented by trajectories rather than static manuals. This establishes Cloud-OpsBench as a data engine capable of harvesting massive expert-level diagnostic traces. This infrastructure unlocks critical avenues for Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) (Ouyang et al., 2022) to align small models with expert behaviors and drives automated prompt optimization (APO) (Zhou et al., 2022), where diagnostic outcomes serve as feedback to scientifically evolve agent instructions (e.g., via DSPy (Khattab et al., 2023)) without expensive retraining.

5.3. Threats to Validity

External Validity. While Cloud-OpsBench covers 7 diverse fault categories, it is grounded in a Kubernetes microservices environment. The specific toolsets may not generalize perfectly to monolithic architectures or serverless platforms, though the fundamental reasoning patterns (resource contention, cascading failure) remain transferable.

Internal Validity. The prompt engineering strategies (CoT, ICL) were implemented using generic templates to ensure fairness. It is possible that model-specific prompt optimization could yield different performance ceilings. However, our goal was to benchmark the foundational capabilities of the models themselves rather than the efficacy of prompt tuning.

Construct Validity. A potential concern regarding the State Snapshot paradigm is that it restricts the agent’s ability to observe real-time state transitions, effectively freezing the crime scene. We acknowledge this limitation but emphasize that for RCA, the “post-mortem” context, comprising Kubernetes object status, time-series metrics and timestamped logs, inherently captures the vast majority (typically >90%>90\%) of diagnostic clues required for logical deduction (Ahmed et al., 2023). Therefore, Cloud-OpsBench is rigorously scoped to evaluate reasoning based on existing evidence, explicitly distinguishing itself from downstream tasks that require trial-and-error remediation or active environmental intervention.

6. Related Work

Evolution of RCA. Traditional RCA methods primarily formulated diagnosis as a discriminative task, utilizing causal graphs or neural networks to identify anomalies  (Li et al., 2022c; Yu et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2023; Yu et al., 2024; Li et al., 2022b; Li et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2024; Lee et al., 2023). The integration of LLMs later shifted the paradigm towards generative diagnosis, leveraging RAG to retrieve expert knowledge for passive analysis (Goel et al., 2024; Ahmed et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025; Xiang et al., 2025). However, most LLM-based methods remain passive, analyzing only provided snapshots without the ability to interactively verify hypotheses.

To enable active diagnosis, recent research has shifted toward agentic workflows (Guo et al., 2024). Unlike static LLM-based approaches, agents are designed to actively reason and interact with complex environments via code execution or API calls. This trend has rapidly permeated various layers of the technology stack, ranging from diagnosing distributed cloud and AI workloads to resolving database failures via expert-aligned reasoning (Zhou et al., 2025; Mao et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2024; Pei et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025; Tian et al., 2025). These advancements collectively signal a consensus that agentic workflows capable of multi-step reasoning and tool utilization are essential for addressing the non-deterministic nature of modern software failures.

Benchmarking in AIOps. Current benchmarks face a fundamental trade-off between reproducibility and ecological validity, which limits the scope of evaluation metrics. Static artifact benchmarks (Cui et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2023; Pham et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2023; Si et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024; AIOPS.CN, 2020; AIOPS.CN, 2021; Lee et al., 2023) rely on offline datasets collected from historical incidents. While offering high determinism, they inherently lack interactivity. Recent works (Xu et al., 2025) have advanced this paradigm by allowing agents to query data. However, this interaction is restricted to generative tooling, which requires agents to synthesize Python code to parse local CSV files. While this tests data manipulation skills, it fails to capture the standard tool-use central to real-world SRE operations. Furthermore, evaluation in this paradigm is strictly outcome-based (e.g., accuracy), ignoring whether the agent arrived at the root cause through valid reasoning.

Conversely, dynamic benchmarks (Chen et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2025; Jha et al., 2025) prioritize ecological validity by deploying live microservice applications. Although these environments support standard tool use, they suffer from inherent stochasticity. Environmental noise, such as network jitter or race conditions, renders experiments non-deterministic, making it difficult to disentangle agent reasoning errors from system instability. Consequently, these benchmarks are also forced to rely on outcome-based metrics, as the non-deterministic environment precludes precise alignment and scoring of the agent’s investigative process.

As summarized in Table 1, Cloud-OpsBench bridges this gap by introducing the State Snapshot paradigm. By simulating standard tool-use via deterministic mocked interfaces, we achieve the high ecological validity of dynamic environments while retaining the rigorous reproducibility of static datasets. This unique combination enables not just outcome assessment, but also process-oriented evaluation, measuring how well the agent’s actions align with expert SRE trajectories.

7. Conclusion

This paper introduces Cloud-OpsBench, the first large-scale benchmark that resolves the tension between ecological validity and reproducibility in Agentic RCA via a deterministic state snapshot paradigm. By constructing a noise-free Digital Twin of the cloud, we enable the rigorous process-centric evaluation of SRE agents across 452 diverse fault cases. Our empirical analysis challenges the efficiency-first orthodoxy, revealing that operational redundancy is essential for reliability and that syntactic rigidity, not logic, bottlenecks SLMs. Ultimately, Cloud-OpsBench serves as an enabling infrastructure for next-generation research, functioning as both a data engine for bootstrapping SFT and a safe RL Sandbox for policy optimization, thereby laying the groundwork for evolving agents from fragile chat-bots into robust self-improving reliability engineers.

8. Data Availability

We have made our collected dataset of 452 cloud fault cases and the code for running the experiments publicly available at https://github.com/LLM4Ops/Cloud-OpsBench.
